subChunks.title: Molecular Biology & Genomics
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora projected a single image: two double helices side by side — identical in structure, dramatically different in effect. One was normal BRCA1 DNA. The other carried a single nucleotide change. “One letter in three billion,” she said. “This variant raises a woman’s lifetime risk of breast cancer from about 12% to approximately 70%. Not a certainty — a probability. Not a sentence — a risk to be managed. Molecular biology reads these letters. Genomics reads all of them at once.”

The transformation from classical genetics to molecular biology began in 1953 with Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins’s elucidation of the DNA double helix. The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) revealed the sequence of all ~3.2 billion base pairs in the human genome. Today, a complete human genome can be sequenced in 24 hours for under £1,000. Genomics has changed medicine, agriculture, evolutionary biology, forensics, and our understanding of life at the most fundamental level.

At SENIOR level, molecular biology is not just about knowing what happens — it is about understanding how we know, evaluating the quality of evidence, and critically examining the promises and limitations of genomic technologies that are reshaping science and society.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
DNA Structure and Replication

DNA is a double helix: two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound around each other, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T: 2 H-bonds; G-C: 3 H-bonds) and stabilised by base-stacking interactions. The phosphate backbone is negatively charged; histones (positively charged proteins) compact DNA into chromatin. Eukaryotic DNA is further organised into nucleosomes (DNA wrapped ~1.65 times around an octamer of histone proteins), 30nm fibres, loops, and chromosome domains.

DNA replication is semi-conservative (Meselson-Stahl experiment, 1958): each new double helix contains one parental and one newly synthesised strand. Key enzymes: helicase (unwinds the double helix at the replication fork), primase (synthesises short RNA primers), DNA polymerase III (extends from primers in 5′→3′ direction only), DNA polymerase I (replaces RNA primers with DNA), and DNA ligase (seals nicks between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand). Replication accuracy: ~1 error per 10⁹–10¹⁰ bases due to proofreading activity of DNA polymerase III and mismatch repair systems.

Transcription and Translation

Transcription: RNA polymerase binds to a promoter sequence (e.g. TATA box in eukaryotes, −10 and −35 boxes in bacteria), unwinds the DNA, and synthesises a complementary RNA strand in 5′→3′ direction using the template strand. In eukaryotes, the pre-mRNA is processed: 5′ cap (7-methylguanosine) and 3′ poly-A tail are added; introns are removed by the spliceosome; exons are joined. The mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm.

Translation: mRNA is read 5′→3′ by ribosomes, three nucleotides (codons) at a time. Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) carry amino acids; each tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon. Start codon: AUG (methionine). Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA. The ribosome has three sites: A (aminoacyl — incoming tRNA), P (peptidyl — growing chain), E (exit — outgoing tRNA). Elongation by peptide bond formation is catalysed by the ribosomal RNA (the ribosome is a ribozyme). The genetic code is degenerate (multiple codons encode the same amino acid) and universal (with minor exceptions in mitochondria and some organisms).

Gene Regulation

Prokaryotic regulation: The lac operon is the classic model — the genes for lactose metabolism (lacZ, lacY, lacA) are coordinately regulated by repressor binding to the operator. In the absence of lactose, the repressor (encoded by lacI) blocks transcription. Allolactose (the inducer) binds the repressor, inactivating it and allowing transcription. Additionally, low glucose activates cyclic AMP (cAMP) production; cAMP binds CRP (catabolite activator protein), which enhances transcription — the operon is only fully on when lactose is present AND glucose is absent (catabolite repression).

Eukaryotic regulation: More complex — transcription factors bind enhancers (may be thousands of base pairs from the promoter) and interact with the mediator complex and RNA Pol II at the promoter. Chromatin remodelling (nucleosome repositioning) and histone modification (acetylation opens chromatin; methylation can activate or repress) control DNA accessibility. DNA methylation (of cytosines, particularly CpG islands) generally silences genes. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) post-transcriptionally silence mRNAs by binding complementary sequences and promoting degradation or translational repression.

Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)

Illumina sequencing (most widely used): DNA is fragmented, adaptors are ligated, and fragments are amplified into clusters on a flow cell. Sequencing by synthesis uses fluorescently labelled, reversible terminator nucleotides — each incorporated base is detected by its fluorescence. Throughput: billions of short reads (50–300 bp) per run; cost ~£800–1,500 for a whole human genome. Applications: (i) whole genome sequencing (WGS) — detect all variants; (ii) exome sequencing (WES) — capture only protein-coding regions (~1–2% of genome) at higher depth and lower cost; (iii) RNA-seq — sequence the transcriptome to measure gene expression genome-wide; (iv) ChIP-seq — map protein-DNA interactions (e.g. transcription factor binding sites); (v) ATAC-seq — identify open chromatin regions.

Long-read sequencing (Oxford Nanopore, Pacific Biosciences) sequences native DNA through a nanopore or via single-molecule real-time detection — reads of 10–100+ kb resolve repetitive regions, structural variants, and phasing of haplotypes, complementing short-read methods.

CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing

CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) is a bacterial adaptive immune system repurposed as a genome editing tool. Cas9 nuclease is guided by a single guide RNA (sgRNA) complementary to the target DNA sequence; it creates a double-strand break (DSB). The cell repairs the break by: (i) non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) — error-prone, creating insertions/deletions (indels) that disrupt gene function; (ii) homology-directed repair (HDR) — using a provided template to make precise edits (less efficient, requires actively dividing cells). CRISPR-Cas9 is faster, cheaper, and more precise than prior editing tools (ZFNs, TALENs). Variants: CRISPR base editors (single nucleotide changes without DSBs), prime editing (“search and replace” — more precise), and CRISPRi/CRISPRa (transcriptional repression/activation without cutting). Therapeutic applications: sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia gene therapy (Casgevy, 2023 — first approved CRISPR therapy).

Genomics — Applications and Critical Perspectives

Medical genomics: Pharmacogenomics matches drug dosing to an individual’s genetic variants affecting drug metabolism (CYP450 enzymes). Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify common variants associated with disease risk — but most common variants have small effect sizes (OR 1.05–1.20) and the combined variants explain only a fraction of disease heritability (“missing heritability”). Rare variants with large effect sizes (as in BRCA1/2) have greater individual predictive power.

Population genomics: Ancient DNA sequencing has revealed that modern humans interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans — non-African humans carry ~1–4% Neanderthal DNA. Genomics is revolutionising archaeology and anthropology but raises questions about the ownership of human genetic data, particularly from indigenous communities.

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) genomics: Companies like 23andMe offer ancestry and health information from SNP genotyping arrays. Limitations: low-coverage arrays detect only ~700,000 SNPs, missing most rare variants; ancestry estimates are probabilistic; health risk estimates are context-dependent. Data privacy is a serious concern — DNA is uniquely identifiable and the information is permanent.

Ethical dimensions: Genetic determinism misrepresents complex traits. Gene-environment interactions are pervasive. Polygenic scores for intelligence, mental illness, or personality conflate statistical correlation with causal prediction. The history of eugenics — including its ongoing resonances — demands that genomics proceed with ethical seriousness about whose genomes are sequenced, whose diseases are prioritised, and how genetic information is communicated and used.

storyBeats.text: Theodora showed a diagram of the central dogma — DNA → RNA → Protein — and then added a set of arrows pointing backwards. “Reverse transcriptase writes RNA back to DNA. Retroviruses integrate into your genome. RNA edits itself after transcription. Regulatory RNAs turn genes on and off without becoming proteins. The central dogma is true but dangerously oversimplified.”
“CRISPR is already being used in people. Is it actually safe at this point — do we understand the off-target effects well enough?”

“For some conditions, yes. The sickle cell therapies approved in 2023 use CRISPR in a controlled way — editing blood stem cells outside the body, then re-infusing them. The targeting is specific enough, and decades of follow-up in similar cell therapy contexts give confidence. For in vivo delivery directly into the body — cutting DNA inside living cells throughout an organism — the off-target and immune response questions are much more serious. The technology is moving faster than our long-term safety data.”
“And the DTC genomics companies — can they really tell me my risk of Alzheimer’s from a spit sample?”

“They can tell you whether you carry the APOE ε4 allele, which is associated with increased risk. But ‘associated with’ is not ‘determines.’ Most APOE ε4 carriers do not develop Alzheimer’s; some people without it do. A SNP array misses most rare variants and all structural variants. And psychological and privacy costs of receiving uncertain risk information without genetic counselling are real. The technical capability exists. Whether it should be sold directly to consumers without clinical infrastructure around it is a genuinely contested question.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing works — from the guide RNA finding its target to the cell repairing the cut. Use an analogy (like word processing find-and-replace) to make the mechanism clear, and explain what could go wrong.
learningObjectives: Describe the molecular mechanisms of DNA replication, transcription, and translation, identifying the key enzymes and their roles at each stage
Explain the regulation of gene expression at multiple levels — from transcription factor binding and chromatin remodelling in eukaryotes to the lac operon model in prokaryotes
Critically evaluate next-generation sequencing technologies, including their applications, limitations, and the interpretation of genomic variant data
Assess the ethical dimensions of genomic technologies — CRISPR, DTC genomics, and population-scale genomic databases — in terms of both scientific limitations and social implications
commonMistakes: Confusing the template strand with the coding strand in transcription — the template strand (read 3′→5′ by RNA polymerase) produces mRNA identical to the coding strand (except T is replaced by U)
Treating GWAS associations as causal relationships — a SNP associated with a disease in GWAS may be in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant, not causal itself
Overstating CRISPR precision by ignoring off-target effects — guide RNA complementarity is imperfect, and Cas9 will cut at off-target sites with partial complementarity at some rate

Interpreting a high polygenic risk score as deterministic — polygenic scores for complex traits are population-level statistical summaries, not individual predictions; environmental factors and gene-environment interactions substantially modify outcomes
assessmentCriteria: Can accurately describe the roles of helicase, primase, DNA polymerase III, and DNA ligase in DNA replication and explain why the lagging strand is synthesised in Okazaki fragments
Can explain the mechanism of the lac operon at molecular level — the roles of the repressor, inducer, CRP, and cAMP — and relate this to a general principle of regulatory logic
Can critically evaluate what a GWAS can and cannot demonstrate — distinguishing association from causation, discussing statistical power, missing heritability, and replication
Can articulate a balanced, evidence-based position on a genomic technology (CRISPR therapy, DTC genomics) addressing both scientific and ethical dimensions
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The BRCA2 gene encodes a protein that participates in homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks. A patient undergoes whole exome sequencing and is found to carry a heterozygous nonsense variant: c.6174delT (a single nucleotide deletion in exon 11 of BRCA2 that causes a frameshift and premature stop codon).

  1. Explain why a frameshift mutation typically has more severe consequences than a missense mutation in the same gene.
  2. The variant is heterozygous — the patient has one normal copy and one altered copy of BRCA2. Why does a single non-functional copy increase cancer risk if the other copy is normal? (Consider the two-hit hypothesis.)
  3. The variant is classified as “pathogenic” in ClinVar (a clinical variant database). What types of evidence would be used to classify a variant as pathogenic, and why can this classification still carry uncertainty?
  4. The patient’s daughter (age 25) asks whether she should be tested for the variant. Identify two clinical and one ethical consideration relevant to this decision.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Frameshift vs missense severity:
A missense mutation changes one amino acid — the protein may have reduced but not absent function, and the change is sometimes tolerated depending on the amino acid’s role. A frameshift mutation shifts the reading frame for all codons downstream: a completely different amino acid sequence is produced from the deletion point until a new in-frame stop codon is reached, at which point the protein is truncated. The result is typically a non-functional protein (loss of function) — especially in a large protein like BRCA2 (3418 amino acids), where a frameshift in the middle of the gene destroys the protein’s entire functional architecture. Additionally, the premature stop codon often triggers nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, eliminating even the abnormal transcript.

2. Two-hit hypothesis and heterozygosity:
Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis (1971): for tumour suppressor genes like BRCA2, both copies (alleles) must be inactivated for loss of function. One germline (inherited) mutation is the “first hit.” A second somatic mutation — deletion, loss of heterozygosity, or another point mutation — must occur in the remaining normal copy in a somatic cell to eliminate BRCA2 function. Once a cell loses both functional BRCA2 copies, it cannot efficiently repair double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination, leading to genomic instability, accumulation of further mutations, and cancer. Heterozygous carriers have a much higher lifetime cancer risk because only one additional event (relatively likely over many cell divisions) is needed, compared to two events required for a non-carrier.

3. Pathogenicity classification evidence:
The American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) variant classification framework evaluates: (i) population frequency — pathogenic variants are rare or absent in population databases (gnomAD); (ii) functional evidence — laboratory assays of recombination repair function; (iii) computational prediction — do in silico tools predict functional impact? (though less relevant for frameshifts — the outcome is obvious); (iv) co-segregation with disease in families — does the variant track with breast/ovarian cancer across generations?; (v) prior published reports — is this variant reported in other affected individuals? c.6174delT is the most common BRCA2 pathogenic variant in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, with extensive published evidence. Uncertainty can remain for novel or rare variants where functional data or segregation data are limited, or where the variant’s penetrance (probability of developing cancer given the variant) is estimated from selected clinic-based populations rather than general populations, potentially overestimating risk.

4. Daughter’s testing — considerations:
Clinical considerations: (i) The variant is autosomal dominant with ~50% transmission risk; knowing her status would allow targeted risk management (surveillance, risk-reducing surgery) if positive, or reassurance if negative. Guidelines generally support testing adults who request it when a pathogenic family variant is known. (ii) Age 25 is appropriate for predictive testing — surveillance and prevention strategies are available and effective for known BRCA2 carriers from the mid-20s. Ethical consideration: The right not to know — the daughter may prefer not to receive information about a serious hereditary condition. Genetic counselling before testing is essential to ensure she understands the implications of both a positive and negative result, and that testing is truly informed and voluntary. A positive result has implications not only for her but also for her siblings and potential children (implications for others who have not consented to the information).
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A genomics company publishes a study claiming that a polygenic score (PGS) for educational attainment, based on 1.1 million SNPs from genome-wide association studies, can predict school performance as well as socioeconomic status (SES) alone, and proposes that PGS could be used to identify children who would benefit from additional educational support. Critically evaluate: (a) what a polygenic score for educational attainment actually measures; (b) the scientific limitations of using it for individual prediction; (c) the ethical concerns with applying such a tool in educational settings; and (d) whether these concerns are unique to genetics or reflect broader issues with algorithmic prediction in education.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) What a polygenic score for educational attainment measures:
A PGS for educational attainment is constructed from GWAS associations between common SNPs and years of schooling (or a related measure). It is a weighted sum of genome-wide SNPs associated at genome-wide significance with the phenotype in the discovery sample. Critically, it measures statistical association with a social outcome (years of education) in a specific historical population — it does not directly measure any biological mechanism related to learning, cognition, or neural function. The variants in the PGS are associated with a complex outcome shaped by access to education, social capital, family structure, economic opportunity, health, and countless environmental factors. The PGS captures some genetic contribution to the heritable portion of variation in educational attainment, but “heritable” does not mean immutable or biologically determined — it means the trait shows genetic variation in a particular environment.

(b) Scientific limitations for individual prediction:
Current PGS for educational attainment explain only ~10–15% of variance in educational outcomes — the majority is unexplained. In practical terms, the predictive accuracy for any individual is poor: distributions of outcomes for high-PGS and low-PGS individuals overlap enormously. The PGS is derived primarily from European-ancestry populations and has substantially reduced predictive power in other ancestry groups, raising equity concerns. The score captures additive effects of common variants — it ignores rare variants, gene-environment interactions, developmental plasticity, and epigenetics. A child’s educational trajectory is profoundly shaped by teacher quality, school resources, family stability, and peer effects — none of which are captured by the PGS. Using PGS to predict an individual child’s “educational potential” would be scientifically unsound.

(c) Ethical concerns in educational settings:
Labelling children early based on genetic scores risks creating self-fulfilling prophecies: if teachers and parents are told a child has a “low” genetic score, lower expectations may generate worse outcomes independent of biology (the Pygmalion effect). It risks embedding a form of genetic essentialism — the belief that genetic constitution determines educational ceiling — which undermines the principle that all children deserve equal educational investment. Consent is problematic: genetic testing of children for non-medical purposes should only proceed in their best interests; using genetic information for educational allocation, without the child’s meaningful consent, risks permanent stigmatisation. Historical resonances with eugenics — using genetic characterisation to sort people into categories and allocate resources accordingly — are not hypothetical; they are documented. Genomics must explicitly address, not dismiss, these histories.

(d) Broader issues with algorithmic prediction:
The concerns are not unique to genetics. Educational algorithms based on postcodes, SES indicators, standardised test scores, or teacher assessments can similarly encode existing inequalities and create self-fulfilling classifications. The A-level grades algorithm controversy in the UK (2020), which predicted and reduced grades for students from disadvantaged schools, demonstrated exactly these dynamics without any genetics involved. The specific concern with genetic PGS is the added dimension of biological reification — the belief that a genetic score is more “objective” or “fundamental” than other measures, which is scientifically unfounded but socially powerful. In that sense, genetic predictors are not more dangerous than other algorithmic approaches — but they are not safer either, and the claim to biological objectivity makes critical scrutiny especially important.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The set of chemical modifications to DNA and histones (methylation, acetylation, etc.) that regulate gene expression without changing the DNA sequence — influenced by environment, diet, and experience, and partially heritable across cell divisions but generally not across generations in mammals.

A genomic alteration involving ≥50 bp of DNA, including deletions, duplications, inversions, and translocations. SVs account for a substantial fraction of genetic diversity and disease risk but are detected poorly by short-read sequencing — long-read platforms are needed for comprehensive SV detection.

Detection of tumour-derived DNA (circulating tumour DNA, ctDNA) or cells in blood — enabling non-invasive cancer detection, monitoring treatment response, and early relapse detection. ctDNA can be sequenced to identify tumour mutations without a tissue biopsy, increasingly used in oncology.

Genomic or transcriptomic sequencing of individual cells rather than bulk tissue — revealing cellular heterogeneity (the diversity of cell states and types within a tissue), identifying rare cell populations, and mapping developmental trajectories. Fundamental to the Human Cell Atlas project.

A statistical method for identifying whether a list of genes (e.g. those differentially expressed in RNA-seq) is enriched for genes associated with particular biological processes, molecular functions, or cellular components — used to interpret the biological meaning of large-scale genomic data.

A method using genetic variants as instrumental variables to estimate the causal effect of an exposure (e.g. LDL cholesterol) on an outcome (e.g. heart disease) — exploiting the random assortment of alleles at conception to avoid confounding. The genomic equivalent of a natural randomised controlled trial.

questions.questionHtml: During DNA replication, why is one strand synthesised continuously (the leading strand) and the other in fragments (the lagging strand)?
options: DNA polymerase can only synthesise DNA in the 5′→3′ direction, so on the strand running 3′→5′ (leading strand), synthesis is continuous, while on the strand running 5′→3′ (lagging strand), synthesis must occur in short fragments moving away from the fork
One strand has more G-C base pairs, requiring more energy for synthesis, so it is made in small fragments to conserve ATP
The leading strand is synthesised by DNA polymerase I (a faster enzyme), while the lagging strand uses the slower DNA polymerase III, causing it to proceed in fragments
Only the leading strand has a promoter sequence recognised by RNA primase, so the lagging strand cannot be primed continuously
questions.correctAnswer: DNA polymerase can only synthesise DNA in the 5′→3′ direction, so on the strand running 3′→5′ (leading strand), synthesis is continuous, while on the strand running 5′→3′ (lagging strand), synthesis must occur in short fragments moving away from the fork
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end of a growing strand — it cannot synthesise in the 3′→5′ direction. The leading strand template runs 3′→5′ toward the fork, so synthesis is continuous in the 5′→3′ direction toward the fork. The lagging strand template runs 5′→3′ toward the fork, so new DNA must be synthesised in short 5′→3′ fragments (Okazaki fragments) moving away from the fork.

questions.questionHtml: In the lac operon, when glucose is absent and lactose is present, which combination of regulatory factors allows full transcription of the structural genes?
options: The lac repressor is inactivated (by allolactose binding) AND the CRP-cAMP complex is bound to the activator site (due to low glucose → high cAMP)
The lac repressor is bound to the operator AND cAMP levels are high
The lac repressor is inactivated AND glucose directly binds RNA polymerase to accelerate transcription
The operator is methylated, preventing repressor binding, and lactose stabilises the RNA polymerase-promoter complex
questions.correctAnswer: The lac repressor is inactivated (by allolactose binding) AND the CRP-cAMP complex is bound to the activator site (due to low glucose → high cAMP)
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. Full expression requires two conditions: (1) the repressor must be off — allolactose (from lactose) binds the repressor and prevents it binding the operator; (2) the activator must be on — low glucose raises cAMP levels, cAMP binds CRP, and the CRP-cAMP complex binds the activator site to enhance RNA polymerase binding. Both are needed for maximum transcription.

questions.questionHtml: A genome-wide association study (GWAS) identifies a SNP (rs12345) that is strongly associated with type 2 diabetes (p = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰, OR = 1.15). A journalist reports: “Scientists have discovered a gene that causes diabetes.” Critically evaluate this statement.
options: The statement is misleading in multiple ways: GWAS identifies statistical associations, not genes; OR = 1.15 indicates a modest 15% increase in odds rather than ‘causing’ disease; and the SNP may be in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant rather than causal itself
The statement is accurate — a p-value of 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ is far below the conventional genome-wide significance threshold and provides definitive evidence of causation

The statement is acceptable because any GWAS signal above genome-wide significance can be taken as identifying a causal gene, and the OR of 1.15 means carriers are 1.15 times more likely to develop diabetes
The statement is wrong because GWAS cannot find genes — only whole genome sequencing can identify specific gene variants associated with disease
questions.correctAnswer: The statement is misleading in multiple ways: GWAS identifies statistical associations, not genes; OR = 1.15 indicates a modest 15% increase in odds rather than ‘causing’ disease; and the SNP may be in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant rather than causal itself
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. GWAS identifies associations between SNPs and phenotypes — it does not establish causality. An OR of 1.15 is a modest effect (people with the SNP have 15% higher odds of T2D, not 15% absolute risk increase). The associated SNP is often not the causal variant but in linkage disequilibrium with it — both are inherited together. Fine-mapping and functional studies are needed to identify the causal variant and gene. Moreover, one GWAS hit does not explain the disease; T2D is associated with hundreds of SNPs, each of small effect, plus strong environmental components (diet, exercise, obesity).
